2db859ece5ee6817.title: The Rising Threat of Great Power War and the Lessons of 1914
2db859ece5ee6817.summary: History does not repeat, but sometimes it rhymes.

ai.sum: A CFR essay analyzes the rising threat of great power war by drawing lessons from 1914.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the post-Cold War optimism that great power war had been overcome has collapsed, as rivalry, nationalism and autocratic cohesion return. Drawing on a conversation with historian Odd Arne Westad, they compare today's dispersing, multipolar order to the years before 1914, when economic and political power shifted and nationalism rose. They stress that wars can begin without leaders choosing them, as escalation logic overrides prudent planning. Their central lesson is that policymakers must understand past mistakes and end small conflicts before they grow into something far larger. They also note that information moves faster and artificial intelligence increasingly places some decisions beyond human control, making the lesson more urgent. The piece is presented as an interview-based essay rather than a set of formal policy prescriptions.
brief.argument: Great power war is a rising risk because today's multipolar, nationalist world resembles the pre-1914 system, and leaders can be pushed into escalation they do not want, so small conflicts must be ended early.

They trace Cairo's restraint since October 2023: it stayed passive as Red Sea attacks cut Suez Canal revenue and absorbed the economic damage. When Israel and the US attacked Iran in February, Egypt sent defensive aid to Gulf allies, including jets and air defence, while pursuing de-escalation diplomacy with Pakistan. The piece says non-alignment brought tourism and investment gains and an energy-transit role, but a July drone strike on Damietta showed neutrality has limits. 2b313abb30585f61.title: Europe’s Defence Coalitions Need Someone to Own the Outcome
2b313abb30585f61.summary: EU leaders are pushing capability coalitions. The next question is who is responsible when the capability does not materialise.

ai.sum: Analysis argues that EU defence capability coalitions need a clearly accountable owner when promised capabilities fail to materialise.

brief.summary: The author argues that EU capability coalitions are the right direction but face an accountability gap: European defence capacity is fragmented across national ministries, ports, railways, power grids, telecoms and private firms, and no institution owns the complete system. Rather than waiting for a single federal structure, he proposes starting with a few willing countries and a limited set of capabilities such as military mobility, logistics, air and missile defence, and surveillance. For each capability, a lead integrator (not a super-owner) would map the delivery chain, expose dependencies, monitor readiness and answer for whether the outcome can be produced. He suggests a 'Defence Capacity Statement' as a common discipline: required effect, usable capacity, critical dependencies, accountable owners and evidence. The Nordic and Baltic states are offered as a natural test case. The core message is outcome first, then visibility, control and accountability, with finance following capacity requirements.
brief.argument: Europe's fragmented defence capacity needs a designated lead integrator accountable for whether each agreed capability actually delivers its required outcome, rather than more coordination or a single common owner.
recommendations: Start with a small group of willing countries and a limited number of capabilities such as military mobility, logistics, air and missile defence, surveillance and energy resilience.
Designate a lead integrator for each agreed capability, responsible for the full delivery chain, unresolved dependencies, readiness and reporting on outcomes rather than ownership of assets.
Adopt a Defence Capacity Statement defining required effect, existing usable capacity, critical dependencies, accountable owners and evidence of delivery.
Map capabilities from the required outcome backwards, bringing civilian infrastructure owners such as ports, rail and grid operators into defence planning while keeping their ownership unchanged.

444ac683e844a78c.title: The Golden Dome Proposal is Destabilizing and Dangerous
444ac683e844a78c.summary: Editor’s Note: This is the second article in a two-part series exploring the Golden Dome for America proposal. Please also read the first, “Golden Dome Is Technologically and Financially Infeasible.”Golden Dome is an ambitious proposal for a comprehensive, layered defense, with ground, sea, and space-based elements. It is supposed to protect the United States, its allies, and deployed forces from attacks by ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, hypersonic boost-glide…

ai.sum: War on the Rocks publishes an article arguing the Golden Dome missile defence proposal is destabilizing and dangerous.

brief.summary: The authors, two physicists who led American Physical Society studies on missile defence, argue that the Golden Dome proposal would make the United States less safe even if it were never fully built. They say a budget in the hundreds of billions and an ambitious mandate would prompt adversaries to add warheads, develop evasive delivery systems, and build anti-satellite weapons to counter it. They add that boost-phase interception would compress crisis decision times to tens of seconds, pushing toward automated launch decisions. They also link the mandate's 'left of launch' attacks and the lapse of New START to rising nuclear risk. Their conclusion is that arms control agreements remain the only approach that has historically reduced the nuclear threat.
brief.argument: Golden Dome cannot provide effective protection against long-range ballistic missiles, and pursuing it would increase nuclear risk by provoking adversary buildups, countermeasures and faster, more mistake-prone crises.
recommendations: Recognise that any deployed strategic missile defence has only limited capability against even a small number of missiles, to avoid hair-trigger postures.
Treat arms control agreements as the only historically successful route to reducing the nuclear threat.
Avoid deploying boost-phase intercept systems that would require pre-delegated launch authority and automated threat assessment.

09fca973c74718c1.title: Who Repairs the Internet in Wartime?
09fca973c74718c1.summary: In spring 2026, Britain, Norway, and the United States tracked and disrupted a covert Arctic exercise off the coast of Norway involving Russian deep-sea submersibles simulating the deployment of a weapon designed to disable the two 1,400-kilometer submarine cables linking the islands of Svalbard to mainland Norway. Svalbard hosts a satellite ground station serving Europe, the United States, and Japan. This encounter revealed that NATO allies can detect a covert subsea…

ai.sum: Britain, Norway and the US disrupted a covert Russian deep-sea submersible exercise near Norway simulating attacks on Svalbard's subsea cables.

brief.summary: The authors argue that subsea cables are a wartime vulnerability the United States has not planned for. Routine faults are handled by about 22 specialised repair ships, but several simultaneous cuts across theatres would exhaust spare capacity and the repair queue, a scenario they say adversaries are rehearsing. They point to the Svalbard interception, China's cable-cutting device, and Russia's deep-sea submarines, and note that repair ships could become military targets, that war-risk insurance can be cancelled at short notice, and that Chinese-linked repair capacity cannot be assumed in a Taiwan crisis. They say the US has retired its government cable ship and funds only two contracted ships. They argue wartime repair should be treated as a national-security mission, with a federal coordinator, a larger funded fleet, trusted spares stockpiles, and tiered escort rules for contested waters.
brief.argument: The United States needs a wartime submarine cable repair and restoration strategy, because its current commercial repair system cannot handle simultaneous cuts across multiple theatres.
recommendations: Designate submarine cables a critical infrastructure subsector and create a federal restoration coordinator with emergency authority.
Expand and multiyear-fund the Cable Security Fleet, procure a government-owned repair ship, and stockpile trusted spare parts at US and allied ports.
Create pre-arranged government-backed war-risk insurance for repair ships before a crisis.
Adopt a graduated protection framework: close escort for government-contracted ships and area security for commercial ones, and negotiate allied arrangements in advance.
brief.turkey: Türkiye sits on Black Sea, Eastern Mediterranean and Red Sea-adjacent cable routes near the Russian and Middle Eastern theatres the piece describes, so the same repair-capacity and contested-waters risks bear on its own connectivity planning.

brief.summary: The authors argue that a generational shift led by Gen Z is reshaping politics in Serbia and Albania, with consequences for Western Balkans security and EU enlargement. They describe Serbia's Student List winning the October election and ending Aleksandar Vučić's long dominance, and Albania's student-led protests against corruption challenging the Rama-Berisha duopoly. They contend that Rama and Vučić had served as Western anchors of regional stability under a 'stabilocracy' model, and that the young protesters are better seen as allies of EU conditionality than as pawns of Russia or China. They warn that the Student List's foreign policy positions are ambiguous and that Albania's violent turn could derail its EU path, and they argue the West should engage on the protesters' own terms rather than through a narrow geopolitical lens.
brief.argument: Gen Z protest movements in Serbia and Albania are a democratic opening that the West should engage on their own terms, since their core demand is political accountability and the EU is their natural ally.
recommendations: Treat the Serbian government's EU reform commitments on rule of law, media freedom and anti-corruption as a test, with scrutiny of Chinese investments included.
Judge Serbia's EU commitment by good neighbourly relations, notably with Montenegro, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Kosovo.
Keep SPAK's protection from political interference as a litmus test of EU engagement with Albania.

recommendations: Prioritise stabilisation, state-building and good governance immediately after any territorial gains.

81215f4922423fae.summary: Can Yemen's army pierce the Houthi heartland? newspress_en Thu, 11/05/2026 - 12:00 Politics As the Iran-backed Houthis seek to capture the city of Taiz and outflank government forces in and around Bab al-Mandab, the Yemeni army is advancing through heavily fortified and mined Houthi rebel positions in Al-Jawf governorate of northeastern Yemen. After recapturing the Huwashiyan mountain in late October, the Yemeni army's Emergency Forces announced further territorial gains…

ai.sum: Yemen's army is advancing through mined and fortified Houthi positions in Al-Jawf governorate as the Houthis push toward Taiz and Bab al-Mandab.

brief.summary: The authors examine whether the Yemeni army can break into Houthi-held Al-Jawf governorate, with the aim of eventually reaching Sana'a. They argue that recapturing mountains such as Huwashiyan and pushing toward al-Hazm would strengthen government depth in Marib, ease Saudi border threats, and force the Houthis to divert forces to defend Sa'ada. They stress that Al-Jawf's tribal networks give mobilisation capacity and that Houthi repression has bred local resentment, so credible military gains could widen an anti-Houthi coalition. The authors caution, however, that success depends on sustaining the offensive, keeping the army unified, and overcoming fortifications, and that stabilisation and good governance must follow quickly. They also note that tribal opposition to the Houthis does not automatically mean support for the government, since tribal leaders will resist both if excluded from power and wealth.
brief.argument: A Yemeni army push into Al-Jawf could reverse Houthi territorial control, but only if it is sustained, unified and paired with tribal incorporation and rapid stabilisation.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Washington's embrace of Morocco's autonomy-under-sovereignty plan for Western Sahara undermines the UN-led peace process and worsens regional tensions. They trace how the 2020 reversal of longstanding US policy, tied to the Abraham Accords, shifted the diplomatic landscape, and note that US backing has been expressed through economic projects, consular moves and efforts to sideline the Polisario. They say this has fuelled Algerian anxiety, prompting Algiers to re-engage in the Sahel, normalise ties with Mali, and cut relations with the UAE. The piece concludes that by choosing a side, Washington may have made regional peace less likely, even as it claims to want to end the frozen conflict.
brief.argument: US backing of Morocco's Western Sahara plan is incompatible with its stated goal of brokering peace and is deepening zero-sum rivalry in North Africa and the Sahel.

fb0a9cb2f2a16859.title: Washington should broaden its Shia outreach in Iraq. Muqtada al-Sadr is a case study.
fb0a9cb2f2a16859.summary: Conversations with several Sadrists reveal a movement preparing to fill a leadership vacuum in Iraq—and engage with the US. The post Washington should broaden its Shia outreach in Iraq. Muqtada al-Sadr is a case study. appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: An Atlantic Council analysis argues Washington should broaden its outreach to Iraqi Shia actors, using Muqtada al-Sadr's movement as a case study.

brief.summary: The authors read Muqtada al-Sadr's October 2026 post addressed to Washington as a signal that he is repositioning as a nationalist, more open-to-the-US Shia alternative to the Coordination Framework. Drawing on conversations with Sadrists, they describe the movement preparing to return to power as the Framework's rule weakens under economic strain, with Iraq's oil revenue losses after the Hormuz closure and the stalled militia disarmament plan adding pressure. They identify two obstacles to his rise: eroded cohesion inside the Sadrist movement after years of withdrawal, and opposition from the Najaf clerical establishment that prefers multiple Shia factions in power. They conclude that Washington should stop treating Iraq's Shia as a reflection of Iran and widen its engagement with non-Iran-aligned Shia voices, with Gulf allies encouraged to do the same.
brief.argument: Al-Sadr is positioning himself as a viable, US-friendly Shia alternative to Iran-aligned ruling parties, and Washington should broaden its engagement with non-Iranian Shia voices in Iraq.
recommendations: Broaden engagement with the range of Shia voices in Iraq rather than treating the community as an extension of the Iranian regime
Encourage Gulf allies, who are closer to Iraqi Shia culturally and linguistically, to engage similarly

852b8c5a4003f540.title: COP31 in Turkey: What to Expect

ai.sum: Türkiye will host COP31 in 2026, with the summit facing pressure to accelerate climate action as the 1.5°C threshold looks likely to be overshot.

brief.summary: The authors preview COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye (9–20 November), which falls on the tenth anniversary of the Paris Agreement's entry into force and proceeds without an official US delegation. They argue that the summit's new COP31 presidency is pushing from pledges toward implementation, with an Action Agenda and voluntary pledges on electrification and sustainable AI. They note real progress, with projected warming down to about 2.8°C under current policies, but judge the 1.5°C goal out of reach. They identify finance, fossil fuel language, emissions reductions, adaptation metrics and a just transition mechanism as the main contested issues. They also flag headwinds such as delays in IPCC reporting and shifting national politics. Their conclusion is that COP31 will likely produce no single breakthrough, though its value lies in keeping climate on the global agenda and building coalitions, notably on methane.
brief.argument: COP31 is unlikely to yield a major breakthrough, and its value lies mainly in sustaining implementation pressure and coalition-building on climate action.
recommendations: Developed countries should deliver on existing climate finance commitments, including the goal of $300 billion per year by 2035.
Countries should accelerate methane emissions cuts, particularly in the oil and gas sectors, where low-cost options exist.
Parties should resolve the timeline for the next IPCC reports so that national commitments rest on current science.
brief.turkey: Türkiye hosts COP31 as president, and the authors' framing of implementation as the test of the summit places Ankara's presidency under scrutiny for delivering concrete outcomes.

(Getty Images) Toggle Table of Contents…

ai.sum: Hudson Institute analysts Tsiporah Fried and Luke Coffey argue the 2026 US midterm results are more complex than a simple Democratic wave.

brief.summary: The authors, two Hudson Institute analysts, argue that the November 2026 midterms were a vote of censure against Donald Trump rather than an endorsement of a Democratic platform. Voters judged his record against his promises, with cost of living as the leading concern, followed by anger over the Iran war, the handling of immigration enforcement, and perceived corruption. They describe the result as a real Democratic gain, including flips in conservative states, but caution that the Democratic coalition is held together more by opposition to Trump than by a shared agenda, and that its factions (progressive, pragmatic moderate, establishment) remain divided. On the Republican side they map competing currents (isolationists, prioritizers, Reaganites, nationalists) and argue the party brand has been punished, with succession to 2028 wide open. They read J.D. Vance's distancing from the president as constrained by his position, and see Marco Rubio's next moves as a test of how much he separates from the MAGA agenda. They close by urging France to abandon ideological readings of American politics.
brief.argument: The midterms were a rebuke of Trump's broken promises rather than a shift to a coherent Democratic ideology, and the post-Trump succession on both sides remains unsettled.

cee614196055884f.title: Putin suffers Balkan setbacks as Russia struggles to retain influence
cee614196055884f.summary: Russia’s recent setbacks in the Balkans are a reminder of the foreign policy challenges facing the Kremlin as the full-scale invasion of Ukraine approaches a sixth year with no end in sight, writes Michael Getto. The post Putin suffers Balkan setbacks as Russia struggles to retain influence appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Atlantic Council analysis says recent Russian setbacks in the Balkans show Moscow struggling to retain influence as the Ukraine war nears its fifth year.

brief.summary: The author argues that a run of political changes has left Russia on the defensive across several regions. A student-led movement ousted Serbia's long-serving President Vucic in a late-October vote, removing a consistently pro-Russian voice in Europe. In Romania, a new pro-EU government ended a five-month deadlock after Bucharest shot down Russian drones over the Black Sea, and the author sees this as providing stability and likely firmer backing for Ukraine. Hungary's Orban, widely seen as Moscow's unofficial representative inside NATO and the EU, lost power in April, and his successor is described as more pragmatic toward Kyiv and firmer on Russia. The piece adds setbacks in Venezuela, Syria and the South Caucasus, while noting Russia's ties with China, Iran and North Korea remain strong and that it is too early to write off Putin.
brief.argument: Recent electoral and geopolitical setbacks in the Balkans, Central Europe and beyond are eroding Russia's influence, though Moscow retains significant partners and room to recover.

c5e12955725a1fc6.title: Last week’s brief Ukraine ceasefire did not stop Russian attacks on civilians
c5e12955725a1fc6.summary: A recent humanitarian ceasefire around the southern Ukrainian city of Oleshky made it possible to evacuate hundreds of residents, but Russian attacks on civilians elsewhere in Ukraine continue, writes Kristina Hook. The post Last week’s brief Ukraine ceasefire did not stop Russian attacks on civilians appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: A brief humanitarian ceasefire around Oleshky allowed evacuation of civilians, but Russian attacks on civilians elsewhere in Ukraine continued.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the brief, localised Oleshky ceasefire, which allowed hundreds of civilians to leave Russian-occupied Oleshky, was a real humanitarian success but should not be read as a shift in Moscow's position. They say the evacuation must not obscure what made it necessary: Russian occupation, the 2023 Kakhovka dam destruction, and mining that emptied a city of about 24,000 people to under 2,000. They contend that staged cooperation, such as Ukrainian and Russian officials thanking each other, reflects Kyiv's wish to save lives rather than trust in the performance, and that the Russian ombudswoman involved is accused of facilitating child deportations. They note that Russian strikes on civilians continued during the pause, including a deadly attack on a school aid point in Zaporizhzhia the day after it ended. The authors call for scrutiny of humanitarian pauses and for continued independent monitoring and accountability.
brief.argument: The Oleshky ceasefire saved lives but does not signal any broader Russian willingness to stop attacking Ukrainian civilians or end the invasion.
recommendations: Keep independent monitoring and accountability in focus after humanitarian pauses end
Do not treat localised, staged cooperation as evidence of a change in Russian policy
Use precise language that attributes responsibility for civilian suffering to Russia

brief.summary: The authors, writing in Al Majalla, argue that the 3 November 2026 US midterms were a sweeping defeat for Trump's Republicans, with Democrats taking both the House and Senate amid anger over living costs, tariffs and the war with Iran. They note Democrats won seats in traditionally Republican states such as Kansas, Texas and South Carolina, while some Senate races remain undecided. Trump downplayed the result and blamed fuel prices and weak candidates, while Vice President Vance placed primary blame on the Iran war. The piece contends that an opposition Congress will be able to chair committees, investigate, subpoena officials and delay nominees, including possible Supreme Court vacancies. It adds that impeachment is possible in the House but conviction would need a two-thirds Senate majority, a high bar.

brief.summary: The authors, writing for Al Majalla, review Philippe Jaenada's Goncourt-winning novel The Unknown Woman of Quai de Javel, about an unsolved 1949 Paris murder. They argue the book's real interest lies less in the crime than in recovering the life of victim Louise Cansot, a Breton model in Montparnasse circles, and in the gap between documentary records and what imagination can reconstruct. The piece notes Jaenada's use of AI in research, which places the novel inside the year's authorship debate, and praises his reversal of the usual true-crime focus from killer to victim. It also flags a risk: the author's interventions and digressions sometimes crowd out the woman at the centre. Finally, it points to the concentration of all four shortlisted novels within one publishing group, Madrigall, as a structural issue for prize diversity.
brief.argument: Jaenada's novel matters most as an act of recovering a forgotten woman's life, using documentary inquiry while openly acknowledging the limits of knowledge and the writer's freedom to imagine.

b932152705f17e88.title: Can Washington and China Build Confidence Around AI and Stability?
b932152705f17e88.summary: In the lead-up to General Secretary Xi Jinping’s September 2026 visit to the White House to discuss, among other topics, AI, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent met with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng at JPMorgan Chase’s New York City offices. At the meeting, U.S. officials proposed establishing a dialogue between the United States and China, which would serve as a mechanism for notification of AI-related national security incidents. Bessent clarified the intent as: “We…

ai.sum: Analysis proposes a US-China dialogue mechanism on AI and stability ahead of Xi Jinping's planned September 2026 White House visit, after Bessent met He Lifeng in New York.

brief.summary: The author argues that proposed US-China AI dialogues and communication channels are not arms control, since they lack enforcement or verification and leave AI innovation and power balance untouched. Instead they should be judged as confidence-building measures, drawing on Cold War precedents such as the hotline, Incidents at Sea Agreement and Nuclear Risk Reduction Centers. The piece sees real reasons for optimism, namely shared concern about AI's role in nuclear decisions, but notes that no AI-triggered crisis comparable to 1962 has occurred, that the two sides define key terms such as lethal autonomous weapons and human control differently, that AI is a general-purpose technology rather than a discrete weapon, and that private firms have interests that may diverge from governments'. The author says the first talks should focus narrowly on the 2024 agreement on human control over nuclear use, sharpen definitions, identify observable behavioural indicators, and avoid contentious issues such as export controls and AI governance. Domestic regulation of AI firms, such as incident reporting, is presented as supporting the credibility of bilateral measures.
brief.argument: US-China AI dialogues can reduce escalation risks only if they are scoped as confidence-building measures focused narrowly on nuclear-related AI risk, not as arms control.
recommendations: Keep the dialogue narrowly focused on human control over nuclear-use decisions and avoid broader disputes such as export controls and AI governance.
Use early rounds to sharpen shared definitions of autonomy and human control, including for early warning and nuclear command and control.
Identify observable behavioural indicators and escalation off-ramps rather than restricting AI development itself.
Build domestic regulatory mechanisms for AI firms, such as incident reporting, to lend credibility to bilateral measures.

bb360b69c4ada491.title: Why Rasputitsa Shapes Operational and Strategic Considerations in Ukraine
bb360b69c4ada491.summary: As autumn sets in, Ukraine's rasputitsa mud season will constrain Russian manoeuvre on the battlefield and strain the railways supplying Moscow's forces in occupied territory.

ai.sum: RUSI analysis examines how Ukraine's autumn mud season will constrain Russian manoeuvre and strain rail supply to occupied areas.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the autumn and winter mud season known as rasputitsa will constrain Russian mechanised manoeuvre in Ukraine, since saturated ground slows tracked and wheeled vehicles, forces artillery onto roads and raises fuel use and breakdowns. They show that the same seasonal pattern has recurred across four years of war and that the 2022 advance on Kyiv was hampered by it. They then turn to Russia's rear support: the occupied Ukrainian rail network is damaged, Russia has built new Sea of Azov lines at high cost, and freeze-thaw cycles, erosion and poor maintenance strain these tracks. Freight and revenue figures for the Novorossiya Railways show declines. The authors expect Russia to lean more on drone and missile strikes, and see little prospect that trilateral negotiations will produce a settlement.
brief.argument: The coming rasputitsa will constrain Russian battlefield manoeuvre and strain its already fragile railway supply network in occupied Ukraine, pushing Moscow toward greater reliance on long-range strikes rather than producing a diplomatic breakthrough.
brief.turkey: Seasonal ground and rail constraints on Russian logistics in Ukraine bear on Black Sea and Azov dynamics that matter to Türkiye's security calculus, though the piece does not address Türkiye directly.

157e7280085f6824.title: Die Integration der CO2-Entnahme in den Emissionshandel der EU
157e7280085f6824.summary: Für den technologischen Hochlauf bietet der Kommissionsvorschlag zu wenig Anreize

ai.sum: SWP analysis argues the Commission's proposal offers too few incentives for integrating CO2 removal into the EU emissions trading system.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the Commission's July 2026 ETS reform, which would auction 250 million extra allowances from 2031 to 2040 to buy permanent EU carbon removals (BioCCS and DACCS), creates the first EU-policy-driven demand for removals but gives too few and too late incentives. Revenue depends on uncertain carbon prices and removal costs, which the impact assessment assumes will fall by 2030 without evidence, and payment-on-delivery sits poorly with capital-intensive projects. The paper warns that a shortfall could push policy toward cheaper methods such as biochar or land-based removals, and toward international credits. Both options risk weakening the LULUCF target and shifting emissions abroad. The authors call for supply-side support and funding instruments to be settled during the negotiations rather than deferred.
brief.argument: The Commission's ETS removal proposal creates demand but lacks the revenue certainty and supply-side support needed to deliver removals at scale, and opening it to cheaper methods would undermine integrity and the LULUCF target.
recommendations: Decide during the ongoing negotiations which instruments will fund the gap between removal costs and ETS revenues.
Add supply-side support such as public procurement, capacity-building subsidies or carbon contracts for difference alongside the ETS demand signal.
Keep the eligible methods limited to durable geological removals to protect integrity, and avoid shifting biomass into the ETS.
Strengthen the forest and land sink through measures such as less harvesting and peatland rewetting rather than relying on ETS-funded removals.

3ea222d1fb724b1f.title: A Green Electrification Target for All?
3ea222d1fb724b1f.summary: COP31 as a Catalyst for European Clean-Tech Diplomacy

ai.sum: A SWP analysis discusses COP31 as a catalyst for European clean-tech diplomacy and electrification targets.

brief.summary: The authors examine the proposed global electrification target for COP31, hosted by Türkiye and Australia in Antalya, which would raise electricity's share of global energy consumption from 20 to 35 per cent by 2035. They note the target is non-binding and not restricted to green sources, which puts it partly at odds with the fossil-fuel phase-out process launched by Brazil. Electrification is presented as a complement to the green energy transition that also serves energy security and competitiveness, especially after recent oil and gas price shocks. The authors describe a balancing act for the EU between cooperating with China, which dominates clean-tech supply, and protecting European producers. They judge agreement at Antalya uncertain, given developing countries' demands for finance, and argue Germany and the EU should pursue bilateral clean-tech cooperation beyond COP31 through initiatives such as Electrify Now.
brief.argument: A green electrification target can advance climate, energy security and competitiveness, but its success at COP31 depends on finance for developing countries and on Europe balancing cooperation with China against protecting its clean-tech industry.
recommendations: Explicitly name green electrification as a strategic goal in Germany and the EU.
Restrict the global electrification target to renewable electricity sources and make it monitorable through NDCs.
Use the Electrify Now initiative as a platform to engage middle powers and trading partners on clean-tech cooperation.
Advance bilateral clean-tech diplomacy to secure markets in third countries and support European producers against Chinese competition.
brief.turkey: As COP31 host, Türkiye is pushing a non-binding electrification pledge whose success will depend on diplomatic skill and credible financial incentives for developing countries.

f15dd44a1c5f0f26.title: Not quite mercenaries: How Russia lures thousands of foreigners to fight in its war on Ukraine
f15dd44a1c5f0f26.summary: Many of Russia's foreign recruits were coerced into service due to vulnerable legal or financial statuses. What should become of them? The post Not quite mercenaries: How Russia lures thousands of foreigners to fight in its war on Ukraine appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Atlantic Council report says Russia recruits thousands of foreigners for its war on Ukraine, many coerced through vulnerable legal or financial status.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the label "mercenary" misdescribes most foreign recruits Russia has drawn into its war in Ukraine, since many were lured by civilian job ads, debt, or pressure rather than choosing combat for pay. Drawing on interviews with foreign prisoners of war and open-source investigation, they describe a recruitment system spanning social media, local brokers, and fee-taking agencies in Africa, Asia and Latin America. They note Russia's legal tools: relaxed citizenship rules for recruits, and a November 2025 decree that ties routes to residence to military service. Coercion of migrant workers and prisoners is also documented. The piece stresses that proving what a recruit knew is methodologically hard, which complicates legal classification as combatant, mercenary or trafficking victim.
brief.argument: Many foreign recruits to Russia's army are coerced or deceived rather than mercenaries, so their legal status needs to be assessed as possibly trafficking victims.
recommendations: Treat coerced or deceived recruits as potential human-trafficking victims rather than mercenaries
Press Russia to stop recruiting citizens of countries that have publicly objected
Ensure legal assessments account for the difficulty of establishing recruits' prior knowledge
brief.turkey: Russian recruitment reaching Central Asia and other regions adjacent to Türkiye's networks is a relevant trend for monitoring foreign fighter flows and migrant pressure.

brief.summary: The piece, a newsletter edition from War on the Rocks, argues that after the US midterms the US-Iran standoff is stuck, with the ball in Washington's court. The authors outline two US options: patience, squeezing Iran's economy through blockade and sanctions on the view that Iran needs time to rebuild its arsenal and nuclear programme, or renewed war, which Trump might see as low-cost and a route to restoring his political image. They note that munitions shortages constrain the latter. On Tehran's side, they argue it will wait a while but not indefinitely, rejecting a no-war, no-peace status quo. They say Iran distrusts US and Israeli intentions during talks and wants guarantees Washington may not provide, and that leaders feel able to absorb more economic pain after years of collapse predictions failed. The killing of the supreme leader and senior officials early in the war has hardened the regime. The text is truncated behind a members-only paywall, so the remaining arguments are not visible.
brief.argument: With the US midterms over, the US-Iran impasse will be broken by whichever side moves next, with Washington holding the initial initiative while Tehran refuses to accept a no-war, no-peace status quo.

bdaaf2d742ef56fc.title: COP31 and Climate Action’s New Centers of Gravity
bdaaf2d742ef56fc.summary: As the world is on track to miss climate targets, governments are grappling with the consequences of climate change. Three think tank experts in the United States, Canada, and South Africa offer analyses on the status of multilateral cooperation on climate action, the importance of energy security, and the role of technology in the climate conversation.

ai.sum: Think tank experts analyse the state of multilateral climate cooperation, energy security and technology ahead of COP31.

brief.summary: Three CFR contributors argue that climate multilateralism is strained by security-driven politics, yet remains essential as the forum for contested questions of responsibility, finance and just transition. One piece contends that solar deployment, driven by China's industrial policy and by energy-security concerns, is the clearest evidence that climate action is shifting from pledges to delivery, while warning that adaptation lags and that atmospheric interventions lack governance. A third argues that the main obstacle to climate action is political rather than technological, citing disinformation and polarisation, and points to information-integrity initiatives as a response. Together they frame COP31 in Türkiye as a test of whether multilateral forums can keep pace with national and market-led action.
brief.argument: The authors argue that climate progress now depends on political will, energy security and multilateral governance, since technology and clean-energy economics are already available.
recommendations: Keep the UNFCCC and Paris framework as the forum for finance, responsibility and just transition questions
Expand early-warning and monitoring systems to reduce damage from climate-driven extremes
Establish multilateral oversight and guardrails for atmospheric interventions such as geoengineering
Fund journalism, research and information-integrity efforts to counter climate disinformation
brief.turkey: Türkiye hosts COP31, so the piece's emphasis on solar deployment, energy security and the limits of multilateral consensus bears directly on its role as host and on its energy-import policy choices.

A recent survey commissioned by Chatham House and conducted by GlobeScan, assessed global sentiment towards Chinese-made…

ai.sum: A Chatham House survey finds European and Canadian consumer interest in Chinese solar panels and EVs is rising despite concerns over China's impact on domestic manufacturing.

brief.summary: The authors report a survey, commissioned by Chatham House and conducted by GlobeScan, measuring global sentiment toward Chinese-made clean technology. Their central finding is that rising concern about China's effect on domestic manufacturing is not reducing consumer appeal for Chinese solar panels and electric vehicles in Europe and Canada; by the authors' account, interest in these products has in fact risen markedly. The piece presents this as a tension between security or industrial worries voiced at the political level and consumer behaviour that moves the other way. The excerpt provided is only the opening of the release, so the methodology, sample sizes and policy prescriptions are not visible here and no recommendations can be reported from it.
brief.argument: Growing concern about China's impact on domestic manufacturing is not dampening, and is apparently boosting, consumer interest in Chinese-made solar panels and EVs in Europe and Canada.
brief.turkey: Türkiye's own solar and EV markets and its trade-defence choices toward Chinese clean tech may face similar gaps between official caution and consumer demand, though the excerpt does not address Türkiye directly.

brief.argument: Affordability concerns linked to the Iran war and tariffs made foreign policy decisive in the midterms, and the president is likely to continue his executive-driven course because Congress can do little to constrain him.

The piece notes that AI-linked firms make up over a third of S&P 500 market capitalisation, so their fortunes shape the wider market and possibly Federal Reserve rate expectations. brief.argument: The midterm-linked selloff in AI-exposed stocks may be temporary if the labour market stays solid and the selling is technical rather than a durable reset of fundamentals.

1e1890c572522b57.title: Putin wants peace talks. He doesn’t want peace.
1e1890c572522b57.summary: Putin is using peace talks, including the US-Ukraine-Russia summit in Abu Dhabi next week, to buy time, not to end Russia's war. The post Putin wants peace talks. He doesn’t want peace. appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Atlantic Council argues Putin is using peace talks, including a planned US-Ukraine-Russia summit in Abu Dhabi, to buy time rather than end the war.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Russian President Putin's goal in Ukraine is effective political control, pursued mainly by undermining Western, especially American, support for Kyiv. They say Trump has offered at least six proposals since spring 2025, which Zelenskyy accepted and Putin rejected or deflected, and that recent US steps (resuming Russian diesel shipments, waiving sanctions in the Graham bill, cutting Starlink intelligence to Ukraine, and entertaining a Putin-Xi summit) have eased Moscow's position. Putin's only concession is a procedural working-level meeting in Abu Dhabi, led by Vladimir Medinsky, whose terms remain unchanged. The authors also argue that Moscow's demand that former Warsaw Pact and Baltic states leave NATO shows the Kremlin still refuses serious negotiation, so expectations for the talks should be very modest.
brief.argument: Putin is using talks to keep Washington distanced from Ukraine rather than to reach a stable peace, and US concessions have strengthened rather than constrained him.
recommendations: Pressure the side that rejects reasonable proposals, as Trump has said he would
Stop unilateral concessions to Moscow such as sanctions waivers and intelligence cutoffs to Ukraine
Keep NATO in the security role of any European settlement
brief.turkey: Türkiye's mediation and Black Sea interests depend on whether Abu Dhabi produces real movement, and the authors' view that talks are procedural suggests Ankara should not expect a breakthrough.

95c3ef3aac7841ce.title: The six strategic mistakes that led to US defeat in Afghanistan
95c3ef3aac7841ce.summary: Twenty-five years on, the United States' defeat in Afghanistan appears less inevitable than the result of decisions that undermined its ability to prevent the Taliban's resurgence. The post The six strategic mistakes that led to US defeat in Afghanistan appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: An Atlantic Council analysis argues the US defeat in Afghanistan resulted from six strategic mistakes rather than inevitability.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the US defeat in Afghanistan resulted from six discrete strategic choices rather than from the conflict being unwinnable. They say Washington tried to build a centralised Afghan state with a national army and Kabul supremacy, backing Hamid Karzai, which ran against the country's history as a loose confederation and fed Taliban propaganda about corruption. They add that the Bush administration's distraction with Iraq left the early Taliban resurgence unaddressed, and that Washington never pressed Pakistan hard enough over its sanctuaries and support for the Taliban and Haqqani network. The surge into Marjah and Helmand, rather than securing Kabul and Kandahar, squandered momentum, and firing McChrystal weakened it further. Finally, they argue the US missed a cheaper option in 2017: using money and contractors to rent the loyalty of regional power-brokers, as Najibullah had done.
brief.argument: The US lost in Afghanistan because of six avoidable strategic choices, chiefly the attempt to build a centralised state and the failure to pressure Pakistan, rather than because the war was unwinnable.
recommendations: Change as little as necessary: work with existing local power structures rather than imposing a centralised national model
Match force posture to the political goals set, rather than pursuing a light footprint alongside ambitious nation-building
Secure the population centres first and farm out outlying provinces to local allies at minimum cost
Use sustained, credible pressure on sanctuary states such as Pakistan, backed by willingness to act against them
brief.turkey: The lessons on imposing a centralised model on a fragmented polity and on the limits of pressuring a neighbouring state that hosts armed groups may bear on Türkiye's approach to Syria and its Syrian Kurdish and PKK-linked files.

1e590bf1c0db4e4c.title: To settle Russia’s Ukraine war, Europe needs to let Kyiv in. Trump can help (really).
1e590bf1c0db4e4c.summary: Any deal to end the war in Ukraine must fix a date for Kyiv to join the EU, but countless hurdles stand in the way. Washington has the leverage to help Brussels clear them—if it can use that leverage in a new way. The post To settle Russia’s Ukraine war, Europe needs to let Kyiv in. Trump can help (really). appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Atlantic Council argues any Ukraine peace deal must set a date for Kyiv's EU accession and that Washington can help Brussels overcome obstacles.

brief.summary: The authors argue that a lasting end to Russia's war on Ukraine should include a credible path to Ukraine's EU membership, since leaving Ukraine in a neutral gray zone would invite future Russian pressure. They note that the Trump administration's own peace plans already mention EU membership, but that the accession process is stalled by member-state vetoes, budget worries and farmers' anger over competition. They propose a US-Europe-Ukraine 'grand bargain': Washington would press Kyiv on EU-required reforms, give Europe a larger seat in peace talks, and offer financing, agricultural market arrangements and investment support in exchange for advantageous commercial and security terms. They present this as serving US economic and burden-sharing interests while acknowledging that enlargement remains an EU decision.
brief.argument: Ukraine's EU membership should be a core element of a durable settlement, and Washington can help unlock it through a conditional grand bargain with Europe and Kyiv.
recommendations: Involve European leaders and key member states directly in peace talks to generate buy-in for Ukraine's EU path.
Coordinate with the EU on the reforms Washington will back and press Kyiv for firmer commitments on rule-of-law and anti-corruption.
Offer agricultural arrangements, such as price floors or purchase guarantees for Ukrainian products sold outside the EU, to ease member-state concerns.
Condition US loans or grants to Ukraine on completing EU-specified reforms.

df97b8c213b78653.summary: Pakistan’s balancing act in a fragmenting world newspress_en Sat, 11/07/2026 - 05:16 Politics Pakistan’s foreign policy is being tested on several fronts. It is deepening its defence partnership with Saudi Arabia and Türkiye, but at the same time it is preserving its ties with Iran, maintaining its strategic partnership with China, rebuilding relations with Washington, and widening its engagement with Moscow. These relationships are not interchangeable. The Mecca Joint…

ai.sum: Analysis says Pakistan is deepening defence ties with Saudi Arabia and Türkiye while preserving relations with Iran, China and rebuilding ties with Washington.

brief.summary: The authors examine Pakistan's attempt to juggle partnerships with Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, Iran, the US, China and Russia. They argue the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye in August 2026, raises Pakistan's regional profile but risks drawing it into long-term conflicts. They say Islamabad must define its priorities, make credible commitments, and keep room to manoeuvre when partners diverge. The piece stresses that Pakistan can support Saudi defence without joining the war against the Houthis while keeping Tehran channels open, and that its credibility with each side depends on honesty about what it can deliver. On Washington and Beijing, the authors argue Pakistan's interest lies in keeping its territory and diplomacy from becoming instruments of great-power competition.
brief.argument: Pakistan can expand its influence through several overlapping partnerships only if it openly sets priorities, makes credible commitments, and avoids being pulled into partners' conflicts.
recommendations: Openly define national priorities and make only commitments Pakistan can resource
Support Saudi defensive security while avoiding participation in the war against the Houthis
Keep Tehran channels open and encourage a negotiated settlement
Balance Chinese investment and defence ties with Western markets, finance and technology
brief.turkey: Türkiye is a party to the Mecca agreement, so the authors' warning that Pakistan must avoid entanglement in partners' conflicts applies directly to Ankara's own commitments under the pact.

a9d1ceda3b479e2a.summary: Americans care about foreign policy. Now Democrats must listen to them. newspress_en Sat, 11/07/2026 - 05:15 Politics There is a trope of US political journalism so time-tested as to nearly rise to the level of a verity: In making their choices, voters in the United States place little emphasis on foreign affairs. But yesterday’s overwhelming victory by opposition Democrats has proved that this falls well short of a rule. One needn’t take this on my authority. On Wednesday…

ai.sum: Commentary argues that US Democrats must heed voters' interest in foreign policy after the party's recent electoral victory.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the November 2026 midterm results show American voters do care about foreign policy, contrary to a long-standing journalistic assumption. They contend that the US-Israeli war against Iran, which they describe as a war of choice inspired largely by Netanyahu, failed on nearly all its stated aims: the Islamic system survived, Iranian regional capacity was not decisively reduced, and Tehran retains leverage over Hormuz oil flows. The piece says the war's costs were felt domestically through higher fuel prices, inflation and interest rates, which voters clearly connected to the conflict, as even Vice President Vance acknowledged. It also argues the war depleted key US munitions and stretched carrier deployments, leaving Taiwan, Japan-adjacent islands, and Ukraine and NATO's eastern flank more exposed. Finally, the authors expect foreign policy to dominate the Trump-Congress struggle over the next two years, since a president who loses Congress tends to focus on foreign affairs, where presidential power is broadest.
brief.argument: The midterm results show that US voters punished the Iran war for its economic costs and that foreign policy will remain central to politics for the next two years.

6b44fbf3d631f093.summary: New Black Sea attacks raise threat of global food crisis newspress_en Sat, 11/07/2026 - 05:15 Business & Economy When Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky warned at the Warsaw Security Forum on 12 October 2026 that a grain crisis could emerge within months, he was not speaking only about Ukraine’s loss of export revenue. He was warning that the war could once again spread from the Black Sea coast to dinner tables far away in Africa, Asia and the Middle East. The official…

ai.sum: Analysis warns that new Black Sea attacks raise the risk of a global grain crisis, after Zelensky warned of a grain crisis within months.

brief.summary: The authors argue that renewed Black Sea attacks threaten a food crisis that would be more uneven than 2022's: wealthy states and those with reserves can absorb the shock, while poor, heavily indebted importers pay through dearer bread, weaker currencies and cuts in aid. They stress that Ukraine's production capacity is intact, since USDA forecasts still show large harvests, and that the bottleneck is logistics: about 90% of Ukrainian grain exports normally leave by Black Sea ports, and Odesa-area throughput has fallen sharply. Grain exports to 16 October were down roughly 25% year on year, with wheat down about 41%. The authors note that replacement supplies from Russia, the EU, Argentina, Australia or the US would cost more and arrive later. They warn the transport shock could become a 2027 production shock if farmers cannot sell and lack cash for inputs. Better stocks and experience with Danube and rail routes help, but they cannot fully replace seaports.
brief.argument: A renewed Black Sea disruption threatens a more uneven global food crisis, driven mainly by logistics and cost rather than lost production capacity.
brief.turkey: The piece recalls the 2022 Black Sea Grain Initiative brokered by the UN and Türkiye, suggesting renewed maritime arrangements would be a relevant reference point.

brief.summary: The piece argues that Israel's 27 October 2026 election produced no clear bloc majority, leaving the coalition outcome open. It highlights that former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, of Mizrahi/Moroccan Jewish descent, could become the first non-Ashkenazi prime minister if he assembles 61 seats, a landmark given decades of Ashkenazi dominance and discrimination against Sephardi and Mizrahi Jews. The authors link the election to Netanyahu's far-right coalition's military campaigns in Gaza, the West Bank, Lebanon, Syria, Iran and Yemen, and cite a leaked Epstein-Barak conversation as evidence of bias against non-European Jews and Arab-heritage Israelis. The argument is framed largely through identity politics and historical discrimination, with the foreign-policy stakes presented as a secondary reason the election matters.
brief.argument: Israel's fragmented 2026 election and Eisenkot's possible premiership would mark a landmark break from Ashkenazi dominance, with consequences for how the state treats its non-European Jewish population.

brief.summary: The authors draw a historical parallel between the 1979 Tehran embassy hostage crisis, which helped defeat Jimmy Carter, and a present-day standoff over the Strait of Hormuz. They argue that hostage-taking remains a core Islamic Republic tool of leverage, adapted from abducting Westerners in 1980s Lebanon and detaining foreign nationals inside Iran. In their account, Tehran has held the strait hostage for over eight months while Iran itself faces a naval blockade. They contend that Mojtaba Khamenei deliberately delayed reopening the strait, betting that economic pressure on Donald Trump would cost his party the midterm elections. The piece presents the post-election acknowledgement by Trump and JD Vance that the Iran war contributed to the Republican defeat as evidence that the gamble worked. The argument is framed as a continuity of Iranian strategy across leaderships and geographies.
brief.argument: The authors argue that Tehran is repeating its historical hostage-diplomacy playbook by holding the Strait of Hormuz hostage to inflict political costs on a US president.

af1b179afff3e106.summary: US midterms: a vote for Democrats or a rebuke of Trump? newspress_en Sun, 11/08/2026 - 04:19 Politics By the morning of 4 November, the US election results pointed to a new balance of power: a Republican president facing Democratic control of both chambers of Congress. Divided government will begin when the new Congress convenes. But did voters give Democrats a mandate, or simply use them to punish Republicans and constrain Donald Trump? From a political sociology…

ai.sum: Analysis asks whether the US midterm results reflect a Democratic mandate or a rebuke of President Trump, with divided government now set.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the 2026 US midterm results, which produced divided government, do not clearly show a mandate for Democrats. Drawing on a sociological reading, they contend that rejection of an incumbent does not imply confidence in the alternative, so voters may punish Republicans without endorsing Democratic policy. They trace a pattern since 2016 in which negative voting, motivated by fear of the opponent, has mobilised voters more effectively than loyalty to a programme. This dynamic weakens parties' incentives to respond to internal criticism and risks mistaking electoral victory for approval of every policy. The piece also warns that when trust in elections depends on which candidate wins, institutions lose their standing as a shared referee. Accepting a legitimate winner's right to govern, they argue, must be separated from disagreement with that winner's intentions.
brief.argument: Divided government after the 2026 midterms reflects negative voting against Trump and the Republicans rather than a mandate for the Democratic programme, and the resulting trust in elections has become conditional on who wins.
recommendations: Parties should not treat electoral victory as endorsement of their full agenda
Distinguish challenges to electoral legitimacy from scrutiny of a government's policies
Opposition and constitutional scrutiny should operate within acceptance of the electoral process

9d2ad7ee64601302.title: Diala Khodry takes on Beirut’s electric wire jungle
9d2ad7ee64601302.summary: Diala Khodry takes on Beirut’s electric wire jungle newspress_en Sun, 11/08/2026 - 04:18 Culture & Social Affairs Beirut’s tangled web of electrical cables has long served as fertile visual material for contemporary Lebanese art, stirring the imaginations of painters, filmmakers and poets who have chronicled the city’s upheavals and crises. Yet the particular significance of Diala Khodry’s exhibition Ishtirak (Subscription) , presented at Art on 56th in Beirut, lies in her…

ai.sum: Lebanese artist Diala Khodry presents an exhibition on Beirut's electrical wire networks as subject matter for contemporary art.

brief.summary: The authors, writing in Al Majalla on Diala Khodry's exhibition Ishtirak at Art on 56th in Beirut, argue that her paintings of electrical cables move beyond the social and emotional documentation common in Lebanese art toward an existential and environmental critique. They contend that in her work the cables become oppressive blade-like structures that shape movement and existence in the city, and that architecture is defined by the void they leave. Reading her central work on rainwater reflections through Baudrillard's ideas of simulation and hyperreality, they describe the sky as lost behind the wires and the water as a brief, fragile breach. The piece also presents her shadows-on-ground work as completing a sense of visual captivity, and its exclusion of historical memory as the source of a melancholy that cuts Beirut off from its roots. The review is a cultural essay with no policy recommendations.
brief.argument: Khodry's paintings of Beirut's electrical cables turn a familiar urban motif into an existential critique of constrained life in the city, using Baudrillardian ideas to frame the lost sky and the melancholy of a present severed from history.

f5c3297a9090d6bd.title: “One War at a Time”: President Abraham Lincoln and the 1861 Trent Affair
f5c3297a9090d6bd.summary: A diplomatic crisis 165 years ago between the United States and Britain over two captured Confederate envoys nearly triggered a third Anglo-American war.

ai.sum: CFR historical piece recalls the 1861 Trent Affair, a US-Britain diplomatic crisis over two captured Confederate envoys.

brief.summary: The authors, writing for the Council on Foreign Relations, recount the 1861 Trent affair, when Union naval captain Charles Wilkes seized Confederate envoys Mason and Slidell from a British mail steamer, nearly provoking an Anglo-American war. They argue that the crisis was defused less by legal merit than by Lincoln's strategic restraint, Prince Albert's softening of London's rhetoric, and the passage of time. Lincoln concluded that the Union could fight only one war at a time, so the envoys were released, and Seward framed the release in a way that rested on the neutral-trade principles Britain had long resisted. The piece presents this as a lesson that the conflicts a leader avoids can matter as much as those they wage. It is a historical essay by James M. Lindsay, republished to mark the US 250th anniversary.
brief.argument: Lincoln's decision to avoid a war with Britain over the Trent seizure, accepting the envoys' release to focus on the Confederacy, was a strategic choice that helped the Union win the Civil War.

ai.sum: An analysis argues that electoral changes have a muted effect on foreign policy, citing historical examples.

brief.summary: The authors argue that elections rarely produce major foreign policy change, and that the high-profile 2026 votes are unlikely to be the exception. They offer two explanations: voters usually rank foreign policy below economic and social concerns, and states have fairly fixed interests and entrenched alliances and rivalries that make sharp reversals costly and slow. Governments therefore tend to adjust existing approaches rather than transform them, and they put their new mandates into domestic agendas. Japan is used as an example, where a new government would likely keep the US alliance, wariness of China and opposition to North Korea while nuancing policy. On Israel, the authors caution against expecting a shift after an inconclusive election. They note that opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot criticised the war on Iran but still backs action against its nuclear programme, and that his Palestine plan would not greatly differ from Netanyahu's.
brief.argument: Electoral change usually yields only nuanced foreign policy adjustments, because voters prioritise domestic issues and states' interests and alliances are structurally fixed.

They argue his influence rests less on public legitimacy than on decades of accumulated relationships, dating from the Iran-Iraq War and a network of wartime commanders that proved more durable than his formal command. The piece traces his rise from a Khuzestan shepherd boy through IRGC intelligence and command, noting controversies such as the Karbala-4 offensive and his rivalries with Rafsanjani and Rouhani. It describes how his 1997 removal from command did not end his access, since he was given the Expediency Council post and kept institutional ties. The authors frame his comeback as a test of how power works in the Islamic Republic.
brief.argument: Rezaei's return shows that influence in today's Islamic Republic comes mainly from long-built personal and institutional relationships rather than public legitimacy.

df3c871ac7421e52.summary: Every administration since the Cold War has been looking for a significant foreign policy breakthrough with China. Spanning containment and normalization to opening and reform, U.S. policymakers have long hoped that China would fulfill its place in the international order and transform itself into a “responsible stakeholder.” Despite years of pivots, new visions, trade arguments and agreements, and other policy swings, the lack of transformational progress is now set…

brief.summary: The author argues that the persistent failure of coercive diplomacy with China on strategic stability stems from status concerns rather than material factors alone. Drawing on social identity theory, she describes China's dissatisfaction with its place in the nuclear hierarchy, reads Xi's speeches and summit readouts as signals of a desired equal great-power status, and sees China's arsenal growth as a means of emulating and competing with the United States. She contends that US demands for prior restraint will fail, and that recognising China as a peer could unlock talks. She stresses this is not appeasement, and that deterrence spending should continue alongside a status-informed approach. The piece presents its case as informed by the author's military and P5 experience.
brief.argument: Recognising China's desired equal great-power status, rather than coercion alone, is needed to move US-China arms control talks forward.
recommendations: Set a tone from the top that treats China as a peer in US foreign policy and dialogues.
Openly demand that China table concrete new proposals commensurate with the status it seeks.
Broaden the agenda to new areas such as AI, space, cyber or undersea activity before discussing capability limits.
Keep deterrence spending while adding status recognition to the negotiating toolkit.

4383aa2a4ab30645.title: Israel’s Foreign Funding Inquiry is Not Evidence of a Stolen Election
4383aa2a4ab30645.summary: The incumbent appears to be using a national security foreign-funding inquiry to discredit 19 Arab-held seats and perhaps disrupt formation of a replacement government.

ai.sum: RUSI analysis argues Israel's foreign-funding inquiry is not evidence of a stolen election and may aim to discredit 19 Arab-held seats.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the Shin Bet inquiry into alleged foreign funding of Israel's Joint List and Ra'am is unfinished and does not justify calling the election stolen. They separate three claims: that some foreign money may have entered Arab politics illicitly, that it explains the surge in Arab turnout, and that it therefore taints the 19 seats and any government relying on them. They find the first a legitimate subject for investigation but the second and third unproven. They note the Central Elections Committee certified results, the law provides no automatic disqualification for foreign funding, and officials say the probe does not affect the outcome. They read the 'stolen election' framing as a political tactic to exclude Arab representatives, delay government formation and favour another election, and warn that a prolonged caretaker period could affect decisions on force, including Iran.
brief.argument: The inquiry into foreign funding is legitimate but unfinished and cannot justify discrediting the Arab vote or excluding its parties from government.
recommendations: Let the inquiry run its course and prosecute any individual who broke the law.
Judge any challenges to individual polling stations on their evidence under Section 86 of the Knesset Elections Law.
Avoid using unfinished investigations to delegitimise an entire community's votes or elected representatives.
Form a government with a settled mandate rather than prolong a caretaker period.

brief.summary: This is a career-profile interview rather than a policy paper. Manjari Chatterjee Miller, a CFR senior fellow and University of Toronto professor, describes how a globally mobile childhood and later study abroad shaped her interest in foreign policy. She explains how her research moved from colonial history in China and India toward power transitions as China rose relative to the United States. She contrasts the pace of think-tank commentary with the multi-year evidence gathering of academic work, and argues that fieldwork, language learning and travel matter for anyone studying rising powers. The interview ends with an account of a chance Harvard dinner that led her to study China seriously.
brief.argument: Firsthand experience abroad, language skills and fieldwork are essential to understanding rising powers like China and India, rather than armchair analysis.
recommendations: Travel widely and learn the language of the region studied
Work in neighbouring countries when access to conflict zones is impossible
Avoid a narrow search for 'foreign policy jobs' and seize varied opportunities

5e285d4e938a35e9.title: Why Belgrade’s new government should not let the Vertical Gas Corridor slip
5e285d4e938a35e9.summary: Serbia’s incoming government should stay the course on the Vertical Gas Corridor to advance economic growth, energy security, and market transparency in line with the Student List’s reform agenda. The post Why Belgrade’s new government should not let the Vertical Gas Corridor slip appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: The Atlantic Council argues Serbia's incoming government should keep the Vertical Gas Corridor project on track for energy security.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Serbia's new Student List government, which took office after the October 2026 election, should not let its September commitment to join the Vertical Gas Corridor lapse. They frame Serbia's energy system as fragile: lignite-heavy power, unreliable hydropower, and gas that is almost wholly imported from Russia via TurkStream at below-market prices. They contend the corridor, which would bring LNG from Greece and Azerbaijani gas north toward Moldova and Ukraine, adds roughly 1.5 bcm a year of import capacity by 2028 and would let Serbia meet its 2.7 bcm demand from non-Russian sources. The authors also argue the project fits the Student List's own platform on transparent contracting, a modern economy and private investment, and so lets the government pursue reform without forcing a choice between Brussels and Moscow. They stress that upcoming tests such as the first capacity auction and tendering will show whether the government follows through.
brief.argument: Belgrade's new government should keep the Vertical Gas Corridor commitment on track because it diversifies Serbia's gas supply and advances the Student List's own transparency, economic and investment goals without forcing a Brussels-or-Moscow choice.
recommendations: Keep the Vertical Gas Corridor commitment on track through the government transition
Use the corridor's first capacity auction and tendering to demonstrate transparent procurement
Ensure the 2028 completion deadline for the Serbian section is met
Use competing supply to pressure market prices and open room for private investment
brief.turkey: The corridor runs through the Balkans toward Moldova and Ukraine as an alternative to Russian-routed TurkStream gas, so Serbia's commitment bears on the gas flows and infrastructure Türkiye is tied to, though the piece does not mention Türkiye directly.

(Getty Images) Toggle Table of Contents Contents…

ai.sum: Hudson Institute authors argue that the transatlantic alliance needs a capital pillar.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the transatlantic alliance needs a third pillar beside military deterrence: control over capital. They contend Europe screens who owns its strategic assets but not who finances them, and that Chinese state-backed credit, buyer's credit, vendor finance and bundled construction contracts can create control that equity screening misses. They also argue that de-risking from China is an unfunded capital problem, since replacing vendors and restructuring supply chains require financing that banks, institutional investors, national public lenders and private capital each struggle to supply alone. Their proposed answer is a strategic capital facility with four eligibility tests (origin of funds, terms, embedded control, substitutability), a replacement window for excluded infrastructure, a European guarantee counterpart, and mobilisation of regional private investors, with US participation via the DFC.
brief.argument: Europe must extend its security screening to the origin and terms of financing and build a publicly backed, transatlantic capital facility so that rejecting risky Chinese finance is economically feasible.
recommendations: Extend EU investment screening to credit and quasi-credit exposures on critical infrastructure above a threshold, including vendor finance, leasing and bundled EPC packages.
Create a transatlantic strategic capital facility with EU and member-state first-loss protection, EIB/EBRD credit enhancement, and DFC participation, with private investors providing senior capital.
Establish a dedicated financing window for removing and replacing excluded high-risk vendor equipment in networks.
Consolidate or interoperate national export credit and political risk insurance agencies across member states.

0675a722cc033e5c.title: Model Citizens
0675a722cc033e5c.summary: The growing political visibility of recent African immigrants in the United States is a standing reproach to dated conceptions of belonging back home.

ai.sum: CFR piece on growing political visibility of recent African immigrants in the United States.

brief.summary: The author argues that the growing political success of recent African-born immigrants in the United States is a rebuke to narrow ideas of belonging across Africa. He points to record numbers of African-born officeholders after the midterms and to high education and income levels among these immigrants. He contrasts the modern, rights-based conception of American citizenship, open to anyone who accepts its founding principles, with African citizenship framed by autochthony, ethnicity and state of origin. He treats the continued emigration of talent as an indictment of African governments, notes that immigrants still face racism in the US, and urges Africans to make their own countries livable and to criticise rights abuses in Africa rather than shielding leaders from scrutiny.
brief.argument: Africa's exit-driven loss of talent reflects a static, autochthony-bound conception of citizenship that the modern, rights-based US model exposes, so Africa must make its own citizenship meaningful.
recommendations: Stop treating Africans as moral aliens and apply to them the same standards of human rights criticism applied elsewhere
Commit to making African countries livable so that talented citizens have reason to stay
Move citizenship beyond ethnicity, religion and state of origin toward equal rights for all nationals

b3aeb28ec4e43d09.title: Dispatch from Dubai: After the midterms, allies see both US resilience and unreliability

ai.sum: Allies in the Middle East, Europe and Asia see US democratic resilience after the midterms but worry about policy unpredictability.

brief.summary: The authors, writing from Dubai after the 2026 US midterms, argue that allies see American democracy as resilient, since voters corrected course against Trump, yet remain wary of US strategic unreliability. Allies do not want a return to any single president or party; they want commitments on security and trade that survive electoral swings. The piece walks through three stakes: Europe and Ukraine, where a possible Trump-brokered deal could cost Ukraine territory unless Washington applies systematic leverage on Russia; Iran and Israel, where the Vance post signals a 2028 positioning away from the war and a likely one-off strike on Pickaxe Mountain; and Asia, where Xi will seek trade and Taiwan concessions from a weakened Trump. The authors close by recalling Truman's postwar bipartisan foreign policy after the 1946 midterm defeat, suggesting Senator Chris Coons could play a Vandenberg-like role.
brief.argument: Allies are impressed by US democratic resilience but worry that American policy volatility now undermines the strategic predictability their security and economic planning depends on.
recommendations: Allies should build economic and security relationships that can withstand US political pendulum swings.
The Trump administration should use leverage systematically against Russia rather than relying on economic inducements in any Ukraine deal.
Ukraine, Europe and their congressional supporters should oppose any deal that betrays Kyiv.

bf6f1f6e1217d16c.summary: Germany faces even more pressure to lead European security amid uncertainty over the Trump administration's post-midterm Russia policy. The post Dispatch from Berlin: What Germans most want to know about the post-midterms United States appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Analysts say Germany faces greater pressure to lead European security amid uncertainty over US post-midterm Russia policy.

brief.summary: The authors report on conversations in Berlin after the US midterms, where Germans focused on how a Democratic shift in Congress might constrain the Trump administration. They highlight concern over the pending Pentagon force posture review, which is expected to reduce US forces in Europe, and alarm at US negotiators reportedly offering Russia discussions on European security as part of a Ukraine settlement, a longstanding Kremlin demand. The authors argue Germany has accepted that Europe must provide more of its own defence, and cite Chancellor Merz's push for European strength and sustained Ukraine funding. They warn that German public opinion, the rise of the pro-Russia AfD, and weaknesses in France, the UK and Poland could limit that leadership.
brief.argument: The authors argue that Germany has accepted the need for greater European self-reliance in defence, but that public opinion and fragmented European politics may not keep pace with the strategic reassessment needed to meet the Russian threat.
recommendations: Europeans should assert their interests through their own strength rather than rely on US security guarantees
Make Ukraine funding a condition of EU budget approval so that all member states share the commitment
Congress should act as a check on any US concessions to Moscow that undermine Ukrainian and European security
brief.turkey: A US drawdown in Europe and possible security concessions to Russia would reshape NATO's eastern flank and Black Sea balance, bearing on Türkiye's alliance calculations and its Black Sea posture.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the planned Abu Dhabi trilateral round between Russia, Ukraine and the United States is unlikely to produce a significant breakthrough, because Moscow and Kyiv remain deeply divided over post-war security guarantees. They read Russia's choice of Sergei Ryabkov and Vladimir Medinsky as a sign that Moscow wants security guarantees at the centre of talks, and that Medinsky's past rounds in Istanbul were seen by Ukraine as stalling. They note Moscow's insistence on its pre-war demands, including NATO's withdrawal to pre-1997 positions and a European security order preserving Russian spheres of influence. The piece suggests Moscow may use the window after the Republican midterm defeat to press Kyiv or extract limited concessions that give Trump a symbolic win. It also points to growing interest among some European states in exploring their own channels to Moscow.
brief.argument: Russia's demands for NATO rollback and a Russian veto over post-Soviet security arrangements make a significant breakthrough in the Abu Dhabi talks unlikely, though Moscow may try to exploit the window to extract concessions.
brief.turkey: The piece points to Istanbul's earlier role as a venue, with Medinsky's 2022 and 2025 rounds there now cited as stalling examples, which bears on any Turkish offer to host further talks.

brief.summary: The author examines Kazakhstan's proposal at the Organization of Turkic States summit in Ankara to invite Russia into engagement with the bloc, and argues it should not be read as simple capitulation to Moscow. He presents Kazakhstan's stance as economically driven, aimed at connecting transport corridors, and as a possible groundwork for a diplomatic push to freeze the Ukraine war, following President Tokayev's remarks to Putin in Omsk. He frames Kazakhstan's search for alternatives to CPC dependence, including a trans-Caspian pipeline, as part of this balancing. He calls this approach "equilibrium in motion," a dynamic form of multi-vector policy, while warning that a concession can become a dependence if poorly chosen and that Russia could use the overture to weaken the OTS. He concludes that Washington should see such flexibility as serving American interests.
brief.argument: Kazakhstan's outreach to Russia is a calculated, dynamic balancing move, not capitulation, aimed at preserving strategic flexibility in the Eurasian heartland.

58c1ba41e7115a9b.title: What students got right about the $6 billion Binance hack, and how they would prevent the next one
58c1ba41e7115a9b.summary: A year before the largest cryptocurrency theft in history, students at an Atlantic Council cyber strategy competition encountered an eerily similar scenario. The post What students got right about the $6 billion Binance hack, and how they would prevent the next one appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Atlantic Council reports that students at a cyber strategy competition anticipated a scenario resembling the $6 billion Binance hack.

brief.summary: The authors compare the October 2026 Binance hack, attributed to North Korea's TraderTraitor group, with a fictional scenario that university students worked through in the Atlantic Council's Cyber 9/12 Strategy Challenge the previous November. They find the students' proposals anticipated several real responses: rapid freezing of stolen funds, cautious but eventually confident attribution, and sanctions aimed at cash-out networks rather than only the hackers. They argue the students also missed two things. First, the real exchange absorbed the losses itself, which raises unresolved questions about who bears the cost of major thefts. Second, the attackers targeted employees through social engineering, while the students' fixes focused mainly on wallet custody. The piece presents the exercise as a way to find policy gaps before a real crisis.
brief.argument: Student crisis-response proposals anticipated much of the real Binance response but overlooked liability for losses and the human targeting of exchange staff, gaps that exercises like Cyber 9/12 can surface before the next heist.
recommendations: Formalise rapid freezing of stolen funds through a standing network of exchanges, analytics firms, financial intelligence units and stablecoin issuers rather than relying on goodwill.
Attribute publicly once evidence is strong, since delay can cost time needed for freezes and sanctions.
Target the wallets and intermediaries that convert crypto to cash, not only the hackers.
Build expedited mutual legal assistance channels with Southeast Asian partners such as ASEAN before stolen funds move.
